question: On the identical completed disclosures, how far apart are native score distributions and paired means?
pattern: Panel a rises mainly in the middle of the score axis for BACE and near its upper end for both comparators: BACE: median 55.6%, middle half 45.2%–65.9%, 8/1,798 at or above 0.90 and 0 exactly 1.00; RAGChecker: median 92.3%, middle half 86.5%–96.4%, 1,139/1,798 at or above 0.90 and 155 exactly 1.00; RAGAS: median 92.5%, middle half 86.7%–97.3%, 1,146/1,798 at or above 0.90 and 233 exactly 1.00. The two comparator curves overlap extensively, including their central ranges. Panel b puts both paired mean differences well left of zero: BACE − RAGChecker: -34.9 percentage points (95% company-cluster interval -36.2 to -33.5); BACE − RAGAS: -35.3 percentage points (95% company-cluster interval -36.5 to -34.1).
meaning: The broad curve separation and the negative paired differences jointly show that the score gap is not just an artefact of comparing different case cohorts. High-end concentration also gives the comparators less room to distinguish already high-scoring disclosures. Similar comparator distributions do not imply matching judgements on each case.
limits: An ECDF higher at a given threshold means more observations at or below that score, not better performance. The denominator is each pipeline’s own claim inventory. A lower native score cannot identify stricter judgement as the sole mechanism or prove greater accuracy. Intervals resample 30 company clusters and do not measure judge randomness.
caption: **Read the figure:** panel a gives each common disclosure equal weight; panel b first subtracts scores within the same disclosure, then bootstraps company clusters. The intervals describe paired native score gaps, not differences in evaluator accuracy.
